endorsements.quote: Chirurgie 4.0 proposes five steps that can genuinely be climbed and a method for deciding, on the basis of evidence, how to climb them safely, with the surgeon retaining final clinical authority at every rung.

endorsements.title: Ensuring trustworthy AI assisted guideline development for clinical practice
endorsements.quote: The move from evidence to recommendation requires the value judgments formalized in the GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework (benefits and harms, patient values, resource use, equity, feasibility), which the system should surface inputs for but a human panel should resolve 1 , 8 .

endorsements.title: Humanoid Colleagues and the Rheumatology Workforce: Preparing for a New Era
endorsements.quote: This boundary supports physician‐led integration: final diagnostic and therapeutic authority remains with the supervising rheumatologist within the multidisciplinary care team, and patients should never be redirected to unsupervised robotic care.

endorsements.title: Structured prompting as reusable clinical tools
endorsements.quote: Ultimately, accountability for any clinical decision rests with the clinician, not the tool: a skill’s output is advisory only, and the responsibility for verifying, accepting, or rejecting it cannot be delegated to the model.

endorsements.title: Reimagining maternal and infant wellbeing through AI-embedded integrative arts-based care: a public health perspective
endorsements.quote: Healthcare professionals and care teams should retain responsibility for interpretation, communication, referral, and clinical decision-making.

endorsements.title: Reclaiming the Human Connection in Clinical Care With AI
endorsements.quote: However, for any use of AI that impacts patient care, it remains imperative that clinicians remain in control of patient care decisions.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence in Family Nursing: An Evidence-Informed Policy Framework for Safe and Equitable Integration
endorsements.quote: Nurses should use artificial intelligence–supported recommendations as prompts for assessment and conversation.

endorsements.title: NeonatAIlogy: The GIRISH (Goal, Input, Role, Iterative Refinement, Safety Verification, and Human Accountability) Framework for Structured, Human-Accountable Artificial Intelligence in Neonatal Intensive Care
endorsements.quote: The AI assisted; the clinician decided.

endorsements.title: Drone-delivered automated external defibrillators in prehospital emergency care: implementation evidence, bottlenecks, and conceptual integration with artificial intelligence and next-generation communications
endorsements.quote: AI outputs should support, not replace, dispatcher assessment and decision-making.

endorsements.title: From Algorithm to Bedside: A Clinician's Framework for AI in Practice
endorsements.quote: The pragmatic clinical implication is that accountability cannot be delegated to the algorithm.

endorsements.title: Multimodal generative AI for pre-practicum mental health support competency development: a human-supervised framework for education-childcare partnerships
endorsements.quote: It may support scenario generation, evidence organization, formative feedback, and reflection, while qualified educators and childcare mentors retain final authority.

endorsements.title: Making periodontal risk visible: the role of artificial intelligence in recall adherence
endorsements.quote: Human oversight must remain explicit, with the treating clinician responsible for diagnosis, interpretation and recall recommendations ( 17 – 20 ).

endorsements.title: [Artificial intelligence and cardiovascular biobanks: Shared technological promise and ethical responsibility]
endorsements.issuer: Revista medica del Instituto Mexicano del Seguro Social
endorsements.quote: En este sentido, la IA debe concebirse como una herramienta de apoyo que amplifique las capacidades humanas y no como un sustituto del razonamiento experto.

evidence.title: Prospective multi-centre evaluation of guideline-based artificial intelligence to streamline multidisciplinary tumour board
evidence.outcome: Diagnosis and treatment-plan changes at 1 and 6 months
evidence.effect: At 6 months, D + TP changes were 14.73% with MTB + AI, 24.3% with AI only, and 28.08% with MTB only; at 1 month: 4.86%, 8.78%, and 13.12%, respectively.
evidence.quote: The combination of the MTB with AI gives the most effective result in reducing the change in D and TP from 28.08% to 14.73% within 6 months (13.12% vs 4.86% in 1 month).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence and the phantom pneumothorax: Clinical reasoning still matters
evidence.outcome: Whether clinician retained final decision authority over AI-flagged finding
evidence.effect: Clinicians overrode false-positive AI alert using clinical reasoning and confirmatory CT; patient required no additional intervention.
evidence.quote: This case also emphasizes that AI should be regarded as a clinical decision-support tool rather than an autonomous diagnostic system and highlights the continuing importance of physician oversight in ensuring patient safety during AI-assisted post-procedural imaging interpretation.

evidence.title: Peer perceptions of clinicians using generative AI in medical decision-making
evidence.outcome: peer ratings of physician skill and competence
evidence.effect: Verification improved vs primary: clinical skills 4.99 vs 3.79; competence 4.94 vs 3.71, both p < 0.001; still below control.
evidence.quote: Presenting GenAI as a verification tool partially mitigated this effect, though the clinical skills rating remained lower than in the Control condition (F(1, 273) = 28.99, p < 0.001, η p ² = 0.10).

evidence.title: Mechanistic interpretability of reinforcement learning in Medicaid care coordination
evidence.effect: In divergent cases, care teams better addressed patient needs in 77% of overrides.
evidence.quote: The 77% where care teams better addressed patient needs validates appropriate human oversight based on contextual information unavailable to the algorithm.

evidence.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Professional Expertise in Adapted Physical Activity Prescription for Orthopedic Rehabilitation
evidence.venue: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology
evidence.outcome: Quality of autonomous AI exercise protocols versus expert-led protocols, informing need for clinician authority
evidence.effect: AI-alone protocols consistently lowest rated (all p<0.05); authors conclude AI without human oversight is not suitable for autonomous prescription.
evidence.quote: AI-generated protocols without human oversight are not yet suitable for autonomous APA prescription, supporting a complementary, expertise-dependent role of AI in exercise programming.

evidence.title: More AI, Less Care-Seeking? A National Survey Experiment on the Impact of AI Intensity on Patient Care-Seeking Intention in Chinese Family Doctor Services
evidence.outcome: Patient care-seeking intention (7-point) by AI integration intensity versus human-only vignette
evidence.effect: Versus human-only, low (β=-0.682), medium (β=-1.053), high (β=-1.267) AI intensity lowered care-seeking intention (all p<0.001); sharpest drop when the doctor deferred completely to AI.
evidence.quote: Relative to the human-only baseline, low (β = −0.682, p < 0.001), medium (β = −1.053, p < 0.001), and high (β = −1.267, p < 0.001) AI intensity were each associated with significantly lower care-seeking intention, demonstrating a graded negative effect.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Enhances Machine Learning Inference in Intraoperative Optical Coherence Tomography Glioma Imaging
evidence.effect: HITL achieved accuracy 94% [88–98%] and sensitivity 98% [92–100%], exceeding model-only baselines.
evidence.quote: This HITL synergy not only improves overall diagnostic performance by optimally utilizing human contextual intelligence over purely algorithmic reasoning, but also ensures that the ultimate decision-making responsibility remains safely with the clinician.
evidence.sample_unit: intraoperative OCT scans (27 patients; 5 neurosurgeon raters)

evidence.title: Diffusion of responsibility: Patient moral judgments of generative AI-informed clinical decisions
evidence.outcome: Diffusion of accountability from physician to GAI in patient blame judgments
evidence.effect: Adherence to GAI advice significantly reduced moral blame directed at the physician (p < 0.001), most strongly for personalized treatment. This is consistent with diffusion of accountability.
evidence.quote: The analysis shows a significant diffusion of responsibility i.e., when an adverse outcome occurs, physicians who adhere to GAI advice incur significantly less moral blame than those who do not (p < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating ChatGPT-5.0 in developmental dysplasia of the hip: A scenario-based validation study against AAOS and AAP guidelines
evidence.outcome: Need for human oversight given LLM errors in ambiguous cases
evidence.effect: ChatGPT overtreated or gave inappropriate recommendations without prompting for repeat imaging in mismatch cases; authors conclude human oversight is essential.
evidence.quote: This suggests that in real-world clinical environments, where measurement variability is frequent, ChatGPT should not be used without human oversight.

evidence.title: Comprehensive Performance Testing and External Validation of an AI Algorithm to Detect and Segment Brain Metastases
evidence.outcome: Rate of AI contours requiring major physician revision
evidence.effect: 46.3% of contours in augmented external validation required major revisions, so authors conclude the tool needs physician oversight rather than autonomous use.
evidence.quote: However, given the notable rate of contour revisions, these findings support its clinical role not as an autonomous system, but as a human-in-the-loop tool requiring physician oversight.

evidence.title: Agreement between artificial intelligence and periodontists in the detection of periodontal bone loss on panoramic radiographs
evidence.outcome: Agreement of AI bone level measurements with periodontist consensus at tooth level
evidence.effect: Across 2,037 teeth MAE was 5.08% points; mean bias 1.61%; wide limits of agreement, lowest agreement in lower molars (MAE 7.66; R²=0.26), so clinician oversight is needed.
evidence.quote: However, the limits of agreement, particularly in the molar regions, were too wide to support the use of AI-derived measurements for individual tooth-level assessment without clinician oversight.

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-generated renal diets by different large language models: a guideline-based evaluation with expert input
evidence.outcome: Suitability of standalone LLM dietary planning for kidney disease patients
evidence.effect: LLM diets were inconsistent in nutrient accuracy, guideline adherence, and personalization; authors conclude standalone clinical use is inappropriate and expert supervision is required.
evidence.quote: Their standalone use in clinical practice is therefore not appropriate; expert supervision and integration with clinical guidelines are required.

commentary.bottom_line: Seven studies suggest that keeping clinicians in charge of AI-supported decisions may improve diagnostic accuracy and plan stability, but only one was a prospective comparison in real care, and none measured patient outcomes such as harm or mortality. Many sources, including FDA draft guidance, endorse the recommendation, while the evidence from tests of the practice is of very low certainty.

perspectives.view: One prospective study in Ukraine (n=728) found 6-month diagnosis and treatment-plan changes of 14.73% with tumor board plus AI, 24.3% with AI alone, and 28.08% with tumor board alone. The other tests are simulations, record replays, or one case report. Plan change is a surrogate outcome, so certainty is very low.

In a neurosurgical replay of 86 scans, clinician-controlled review reached 94% accuracy and 98% sensitivity, above model-only baselines. A case report describes clinicians overriding a false-positive alert. A hazard study found 46.3% of AI contours needed major revision, which shows the failure mode exists but does not show that retained authority catches it.

A replay of 250,000 decision records found care teams better addressed patient needs in 77% of divergent overrides. In a vignette study of 276 clinicians, physicians who used AI to verify their work received higher peer skill ratings (4.99 vs 3.79) than those who relied on it primarily, but their ratings stayed below the control condition.

The 250,000-record replay drew on a Medicaid population, and the Ukrainian deployment included rural patients. No test enrolled safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Two hazard studies involving limited English or non-English populations found LLM errors in imaging cases and kidney diet plans, but neither tested whether clinician authority prevents those errors.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software states that a tool should not replace standard-of-care diagnosis and should be applied jointly with clinician judgment. In a vignette study of 331 participants, following AI advice reduced blame directed at the physician (p < 0.001), which suggests that perceived accountability may shift away from clinicians who defer to AI.

In a vignette study of 2,790 participants in China, care-seeking intention fell as AI involvement rose, from β=-0.682 at low intensity to β=-1.267 at high intensity, with the largest drop when the doctor deferred fully to AI. Visible clinician authority may matter to patient trust, although vignettes may not predict real behavior.

commentary.research_gap: No randomized or controlled deployment study has compared retained clinician authority with more autonomous AI use on patient outcomes such as diagnostic error, harm, or mortality. No study has tested whether labeling AI tools as adjuncts changes clinician behavior or patient understanding. No study has measured the time, staffing, or cost burden of clinician review at scale.
commentary.underserved_note: One test, a retrospective replay of 250,000 decision records, drew on a Medicaid population, and the Ukrainian deployment included rural patients. No test of the practice included safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore cannot show whether clinician override works as well in settings where language barriers or thin staffing may limit review.
